case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):

  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis.
